part2.intro: Three young people talk about a sporting challenge they did.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Jamal
texts.text: Last year I swam five kilometres in the sea to raise money for a children's hospital. It took me nearly two hours! The water temperature was only fifteen degrees, so I wore a special suit. My uncle swam next to me the whole time. My arms hurt for a week afterwards, but we raised eight hundred pounds, so it was worth it.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Anya
texts.text: I'm in the school high jump team. When I started two years ago, I could only jump one metre. Now I can jump one metre fifty-five centimetres! I practise for an hour every day after school, and my coach says I could be in the national team in a few years. My next competition is in three weeks.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Duc
texts.text: Last summer my dad and I cycled from our home in Leeds to my grandma's house in London. It's about two hundred miles, and we did it in four days. Every evening we stayed in a small hotel. On the second day it rained for hours and I wanted to stop, but Dad made me laugh and we kept going. It was the best week of the year!

items.q: Who did their challenge to help other people?
Who did their challenge in cold water?
Who trains every day?
Who nearly gave up?
Who hopes to do well at a higher level in the future?
Who felt pain after their challenge?
Who slept away from home during their challenge?

part3.title: The girl who loves the weather
part3.text:
Every morning at seven o'clock, before breakfast, thirteen-year-old Isla Grant goes out into her garden with a notebook. She isn't looking at the flowers – she's checking the weather.

Isla has her own small weather station. It measures the temperature, the rain and the wind. "My grandad gave it to me for my tenth birthday," she says. "He was a farmer, so the weather was really important for his work. At first I only looked at it for a few minutes a week, but soon I was checking it every day."

Isla writes everything in her notebook and then puts it on a website for weather fans. Last year she recorded a hundred and ten centimetres of rain. The coldest day was in January, when it was minus eight degrees. The hottest was in July: thirty-one degrees. "That's very hot for Scotland!" she laughs.

Last month, a local radio station heard about Isla and asked her to give the weather news every Saturday morning. "I was really worried the first time," she says. "I only had ninety seconds, and I spoke too quickly. But now I enjoy it."

Isla wants to study weather at university. "People think it's boring, but the weather changes every hour of every day," she says. "You never know what's coming next. That's why I love it!"

items.q: What does Isla do every morning?
options: She has breakfast in the garden.
She writes down information about the weather.

items.q: What do we learn about Isla's grandad?
options: The weather was important for his job.
He checks the weather station every day.

items.q: What does Isla say about last year?
options: One day in July was very hot.
There was less rain than usual.

items.q: How did Isla feel the first time she was on the radio?
Why does Isla love the weather?
options: It helps her with her school work.

part4.title: The marathon
part4.text:
The marathon is a running race of just over forty-two kilometres, or about twenty-six miles. The story {19} that thousands of years ago, a Greek soldier ran all the way from the town of Marathon to Athens with some important news.

The first Olympic marathon {20} place in Athens in 1896. The distance changed a few times after that, but in 1921 it became the {21} we use today.

Today, the fastest runners can finish a marathon in just over two hours, but most people take between four and five hours. Runners usually {22} for months before a big race. On the day, they must drink lots of water, because they can lose more than two litres {23} the race, especially when the temperature is high.

Many big cities, like London and New York, have a marathon every year. Thousands of people take part, and some of them run in funny clothes to {24} money for children's hospitals and other charities.

items.q: How far did the girl run this morning?

script.t: You look tired, Sara. Did you go running this morning?
Yes. Usually I run two kilometres around the park, but today I did five.
Wow! Are you training for the big race?
Yes, the ten-kilometre race in May. I've got two months to get ready!

items.q: What is the temperature today?

script.t: Shall we have lunch in the garden? It's sunny.
It's sunny, but it's only twelve degrees. Yesterday it was twenty-one!
Really? The radio said it would be eighteen today.
Well, the radio was wrong. Let's eat inside and go out later.

items.q: How much milk does the boy need?

script.t: Mum, I'm making pancakes for everyone. Is there any milk?
There's half a litre in the fridge. Is that enough?
The recipe says one litre for four people, but there are eight of us today with Grandma and Grandpa and the cousins.
So you need two litres. I'll go to the shop.

items.q: What time does the swimming lesson start?

script.t: Hurry up, Tom! Your swimming lesson starts at quarter past four.
No, Mum, they changed it. It's at half past four now.
Oh, OK. But it takes fifteen minutes to get there, and it's already quarter to four.
That's fine. We've got lots of time.

items.q: How tall is the boy now?

script.t: Let's see how tall you are now, Ben. Stand still against the door for a moment.
Last year I was one metre forty-five.
Well, now you're one metre fifty-two! You've grown seven centimetres.
Great! I want to be one metre sixty, like my brother.

part2.intro: You will hear a teacher telling students about a charity walk.
part2.title: School Charity Walk

script.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Next Saturday our school is having a charity walk to raise money for the town hospital. Last year the walk was eight kilometres, but this year it's longer – twelve kilometres. Don't worry, there'll be lots of stops! We'll meet at quarter to nine outside the railway station, not at school. The weather report says it will be warm – about twenty-four degrees – so please bring at least two litres of water. Half a litre isn't enough! Wear comfortable shoes and a hat. We'll stop for lunch after about six kilometres. We thought about having lunch at the café in the village, but it's too small for a hundred students. So we'll eat at a farm near the river, where you can buy sandwiches and drinks. We'll finish at about four o'clock, and your parents can collect you from the park. If you have any questions, please ask Mr Fletcher. That's F-L-E-T-C-H-E-R. He's organising the walk this year. And don't forget to collect your form from the school office this week.

part3.intro: You will hear Leo talking to his friend Amy about a cycling race.

items.q: How long is the race for Leo's age group?
How often does Leo train now?
What is Leo's problem when he cycles?
options: He can't go up hills quickly.

items.q: What does Amy suggest?
What time does Leo's race start?

script.t: Hi Leo. Are you still doing the cycling race next month?
Yes! I'm really excited about it.
Is it fifty kilometres, like last year? My brother did that one.
That's the adults' race. Some of them do eighty kilometres! It's shorter for under-fifteens. We only do thirty kilometres – that's about eighteen miles.
That's still a long way. Are you training a lot?
I'd like to train every day, but I've got too much homework. Before, I only went out twice a week. Now I go three times – on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday.
Is your bike OK? It looks quite heavy.
It's about twelve kilos, which is fine. And I'm quite good on hills. My real problem is the heat. When it's more than thirty degrees, I feel terrible after a few minutes.
Why don't you train before school, when it's cooler? You could go out at half past six.
That's a good idea. I already drink lots of water, but that doesn't help much.
So when does the race start?
The adults start at half past nine, and we start forty-five minutes later, at quarter past ten. But I need to be there at eight o'clock to get my number.
I'll come and watch you!

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking to his mum about a recipe.
items.q: What is the problem?

script.t: Mum, this recipe is from an American website. It says two cups of flour and one stick of butter. How many grams is that? Our scales only show grams and kilos!
Hmm, I'm not sure. Let me look on my phone.
Thanks. I've got all the eggs, and the oven's already at a hundred and eighty degrees.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking about a holiday.
items.q: What did she enjoy most?

script.t: We drove eight hundred kilometres to the mountains. It took two days, which was really boring. The temperature was nearly thirty-five degrees every day – too hot for me. But on the last day we climbed to the top of a mountain, two thousand metres high. The view was amazing. I'll never forget it!

items.intro: You will hear a man on the radio talking about the weather.
items.q: What will the weather be like at the weekend?

script.t: It's been a lovely warm week, with temperatures of around twenty-two degrees. But get your coats ready! On Saturday and Sunday it'll only be ten or eleven degrees, and there'll be strong winds. The warm weather won't come back until next Wednesday.

items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a phone app.
items.q: Why does the girl like the app?
options: It shows how far she walks.

script.t: Look at this app. It counts how many steps I take and how many kilometres I walk every day. Yesterday I walked seven kilometres!
Cool. Does it tell you how many hours you sleep, too?
It can, but I don't use that. I just love seeing how far I've gone each day.

items.intro: You will hear a girl leaving a message for her friend.
items.q: Why is she calling?

to change where they will meet
to ask her friend to bring something

script.t: Hi Jess, it's Mai. About the cinema tonight – the film still starts at seven, but let's not meet outside the cinema, because it's going to rain. Let's meet in the café opposite instead, at quarter to seven. I'll get there a few minutes early and buy the tickets. See you!

part5.intro: You will hear Josh talking to his grandmother about Sports Day at his school. Which event did each person win?

script.t: How was Sports Day, Josh? Did your friends win anything?
Yes, lots! Ali won the three-kilometre run. He finished in eleven minutes – nearly a minute before everyone else.
Wonderful. Wasn't he in the eight hundred metres too?
He wanted to be, but you can only do two events, so he chose the relay race. His team came second.
And Hannah? She's very good at the long jump, isn't she?
She usually is, but this time she came third in that. She won the high jump, though – she jumped one metre forty!
Clever girl. And what about Kevin?
Kevin won the hundred metres. It took him only thirteen seconds. Everyone was cheering.
And your sister? Lucy's a good runner.
She hurt her leg last week, so she couldn't run. But she won the fifty-metre swimming race in the pool.
And you, Josh?
I wasn't fast enough for any of the races. But I won the ball throwing! I threw it thirty-five metres.
Well done, Josh! I'm very proud of you. Let's have some cake to celebrate.
